claim: Injectisomes are multi-protein transmembrane machines allowing pathogenic bacteria to inject effector proteins into eukaryotic host cells.
source: Injectisomes are multi-protein transmembrane machines allowing pathogenic bacteria to inject effector proteins into eukaryotic host cells, a process called type III secretion.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about injectisomes and type III secretion systems.

claim: This is the first three-dimensional structure of Yersinia enterocolitica injectisomes in situ.
source: Here we present the first three-dimensional structure of Yersinia enterocolitica and Shigella flexneri injectisomes in situ and the first structural analysis of the Yersinia injectisome.
evidence: The manuscript presents novel structural data obtained through cryo-ET experiments.

claim: This is the first three-dimensional structure of Shigella flexneri injectisomes in situ.
source: Here we present the first three-dimensional structure of Yersinia enterocolitica and Shigella flexneri injectisomes in situ and the first structural analysis of the Yersinia injectisome.
evidence: The manuscript presents novel structural data obtained through cryo-ET experiments.

claim: This is the first structural analysis of the Yersinia injectisome.
source: Here we present the first three-dimensional structure of Yersinia enterocolitica and Shigella flexneri injectisomes in situ and the first structural analysis of the Yersinia injectisome.
evidence: The manuscript presents novel structural data obtained through cryo-ET experiments.

claim: Basal bodies of injectisomes inside bacterial cells showed length variations of 20%.
source: Unexpectedly, basal bodies of injectisomes inside the bacterial cells showed length variations of 20%.
evidence: This is supported by MRA classification data showing intermembrane distances ranging from 30 to 36 nm.

claim: The in situ structures of Y. enterocolitica and S. flexneri injectisomes had similar dimensions.
source: The in situ structures of the Y. enterocolitica and S. flexneri injectisomes had similar dimensions and were significantly longer than the isolated structures of related injectisomes.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET reconstructions showing both have ~32-33 nm intermembrane distances.

claim: The in situ structures of Y. enterocolitica and S. flexneri injectisomes were significantly longer than the isolated structures of related injectisomes.
source: The in situ structures of the Y. enterocolitica and S. flexneri injectisomes had similar dimensions and were significantly longer than the isolated structures of related injectisomes.
evidence: Comparison with isolated structures from Salmonella and Shigella shows ~10 nm difference in length.

claim: The crystal structure of YscD appeared elongated compared to a homologous protein.
source: The crystal structure of the inner membrane injectisome component YscD appeared elongated compared to a homologous protein, and molecular dynamics simulations documented its elongation elasticity.
evidence: X-ray crystallography data shows YscD has an extended conformation compared to PrgH.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations documented the elongation elasticity of YscD.
source: The crystal structure of the inner membrane injectisome component YscD appeared elongated compared to a homologous protein, and molecular dynamics simulations documented its elongation elasticity.
evidence: MD simulations show YscD can undergo barrier-free transition between compact and extended conformations.

claim: The ring-shaped secretin YscC at the outer membrane was stretched by 30-40% in situ compared to its isolated liposome-embedded conformation.
source: The ring-shaped secretin YscC at the outer membrane was stretched by 30–40% in situ, compared to its isolated liposome-embedded conformation.
evidence: Comparison of in situ cryo-ET structure with isolated YscC reconstituted in liposomes shows this extension.

claim: Elasticity is critical for some two-membrane spanning protein complexes to cope with variations in the intermembrane distance.
source: We suggest that elasticity is critical for some two-membrane spanning protein complexes to cope with variations in the intermembrane distance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed structural flexibility and osmotic stress experiments.

claim: The bacterial type III secretion apparatus allows Gram-negative bacteria to export effector proteins in one step across the two bacterial membranes and an eukaryotic cell membrane.
source: The bacterial type III secretion apparatus, the injectisome, is a complex nanomachine that allows Gram-negative bacteria to export effector proteins in one step across the two bacterial membranes and an eukaryotic cell membrane (Cornelis, 2006; Galan and Wolf-Watz, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The assembly of the injectisome involves some 34 different proteins.
source: The assembly of the injectisome involves some 34 different proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about injectisome composition.

claim: Phylogenic analyses classify injectisomes into seven different families.
source: Phylogenic analyses based on the most conserved proteins classify injectisomes into seven different families (Ysc, Ssa-Esc, Inv-Mxi-Spa, Hrc1, Hrc2, Rhizobiales, and Chlamydiales) (Pallen et al., 2005; Troisfontaines and Cornelis, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: The injectisome consists of a ~60 nm long, hollow needle protruding from the bacterial surface.
source: The injectisome consists of three parts: a ∼60 nm long, hollow needle protruding from the bacterial surface, a basal body that spans the two bacterial membranes and the periplasm, and a cytoplasmic part.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about injectisomes.

claim: The injectisome consists of a basal body that spans the two bacterial membranes and the periplasm.
source: The injectisome consists of three parts: a ∼60 nm long, hollow needle protruding from the bacterial surface, a basal body that spans the two bacterial membranes and the periplasm, and a cytoplasmic part.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about injectisomes.

claim: The injectisome consists of a cytoplasmic part.
source: The injectisome consists of three parts: a ∼60 nm long, hollow needle protruding from the bacterial surface, a basal body that spans the two bacterial membranes and the periplasm, and a cytoplasmic part.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about injectisomes.

claim: The basal body presents a barrel-shaped structure at the outer membrane.
source: The basal body presents a barrel-shaped structure at the outer membrane (OM), with double ring-shaped densities underneath in the periplasmic space and the inner membrane (IM).
evidence: This is established from previous structural studies of isolated basal bodies.

claim: The basal body has double ring-shaped densities in the periplasmic space and the inner membrane.
source: The basal body presents a barrel-shaped structure at the outer membrane (OM), with double ring-shaped densities underneath in the periplasmic space and the inner membrane (IM).
evidence: This is established from previous structural studies of isolated basal bodies.

claim: The barrel-shaped structure spanning the OM consists of a 12-15 mer of a protein from the secretin family.
source: The barrel-shaped structure spanning the OM and protruding into the periplasm consists of a 12–15 mer of a protein from the secretin family (YscC, InvG, MxiD) (Burghout et al., 2004; Marlovits et al., 2004; Hodgkinson et al., 2009; Spreter et al., 2009; Schraidt and Marlovits, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: YscJ is proposed to form a 24-subunit ring.
source: The lower double-ring reaching into the IM is made of a lipoprotein (YscJ, PrgK, MxiJ) proposed to form a 24-subunit ring (Kimbrough and Miller, 2000; Crepin et al., 2005; Yip et al., 2005; Silva-Herzog et al., 2008; Hodgkinson et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The injectisome is evolutionarily related to the bacterial flagellar motor system.
source: The injectisome is evolutionarily related to the bacterial flagellar motor system, with which it shares the basic type III secretion export apparatus (Cornelis, 2006; Minamino et al., 2008; Erhardt et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to evolutionary studies.

claim: Cryo electron tomography was applied to visualize injectisomes in intact Yersinia enterocolitica cells at nanometer-scale resolution.
source: We applied cryo electron tomography (cryo-ET) to visualize injectisomes in intact Yersinia enterocolitica cells at nanometer-scale resolution and found variations in their appearance (Figure 1), indicating an intrinsic flexibility.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Variations in injectisome appearance indicate an intrinsic flexibility.
source: We applied cryo electron tomography (cryo-ET) to visualize injectisomes in intact Yersinia enterocolitica cells at nanometer-scale resolution and found variations in their appearance (Figure 1), indicating an intrinsic flexibility.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed structural variations.

claim: Y. enterocolitica minicells were genetically engineered to be thinner and still have assembled injectisomes.
source: Since thick cells reduced the quality of tomographic imaging, we genetically engineered Y. enterocolitica minicells that were thinner and still had assembled injectisomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach to improve imaging quality.

claim: Reduced thickness allowed for imaging conditions permitting a higher resolution reconstruction.
source: Reduced thickness allowed for imaging conditions permitting a higher resolution reconstruction (Kudryashev et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a methodological paper and the experimental results.

claim: Sub-tomogram averaging yielded a reconstruction of the injectisome in situ at ~4 nm resolution.
source: Sub-tomogram averaging of volumes containing injectisomes from tomograms of Y. enterocolitica minicells and focal pair tomograms (Kudryashev et al., 2012b) of wild type, regularly sized cells were performed using a customized local feature alignment strategy to compensate for structural variations among individual injectisomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, 'Materials and methods' for details). This yielded a reconstruction of the injectisome in situ at ∼4 nm resolution (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by FSC analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The vertical distance between the centers of the membranes in the reconstruction is ~33 nm.
source: The vertical distance between the centers of the membranes in the reconstruction is ∼33 nm.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the cryo-ET reconstruction.

claim: The measured intermembrane distance is significantly larger than the ~20 nm expected from the structures of basal bodies isolated from Salmonella enterica SPI-I and S. flexneri.
source: This average value is in the range of values reported for gram-negative bacteria (Chen et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012), but significantly larger than the ∼20 nm expected from the structures of basal bodies isolated from Salmonella enterica SPI-I and S. flexneri (Hodgkinson et al., 2009; Schraidt and Marlovits, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published structures and citations.

claim: CEMOVIS imaging confirmed the intra-membrane distance.
source: Independent measurements made by imaging Y. enterocolitica cells by cryo-electron microscopy of vitreous sections (CEMOVIS) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and 'Materials and methods') and tomography on high pressure frozen and freeze substituted bacteria (data not shown) confirmed the intra-membrane distance.
evidence: This is supported by independent measurements using a different technique.

claim: The largest lateral diameter of the periplasmic part of the average injectisome structure is 18 nm.
source: Measuring from mass center to mass center, the largest lateral diameter of the periplasmic part of the average injectisome structure is 18 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the reconstruction.

claim: The largest diameter at the outer OM is 12 nm.
source: The largest diameter at the outer OM is 12 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), which is in good agreement with the dimensions of isolated and liposome reconstituted YscC complexes (see below).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the reconstruction.

claim: Classification by iterative multi reference alignment revealed intermembrane distances ranged from 30 to 36 nm.
source: Classification by iterative multi reference alignment (MRA) of individual in situ Y. enterocolitica injectisomes revealed large variations in the length of the complex in the intermembrane space; intermembrane distances ranged from 30 to 36 nm (Figure 2B–C), suggesting that the basal body of the injectisome is highly flexible in the cellular context.
evidence: This is supported by MRA classification data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The basal body of the injectisome is highly flexible in the cellular context.
source: Classification by iterative multi reference alignment (MRA) of individual in situ Y. enterocolitica injectisomes revealed large variations in the length of the complex in the intermembrane space; intermembrane distances ranged from 30 to 36 nm (Figure 2B–C), suggesting that the basal body of the injectisome is highly flexible in the cellular context.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed length variations.

claim: The 2.7 Å resolution structure of YscD150–362 showed three linearly arranged domains.
source: The 2.7 Å resolution structure of YscD150–362 (Supplementary file 1A) showed three linearly arranged domains (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray crystallography data.

claim: Each domain of YscD comprises an αββαβ-ring building motif.
source: Each domain comprises an αββαβ-ring building motif, which superposes well with corresponding motifs in the three domains of the homologous PrgH from Salmonella enterica (Spreter et al., 2009) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and comparison with PrgH.

claim: YscD features an extended conformation while the domains of PrgH are in a more compact arrangement.
source: However, although sharing the same multi-domain architecture, YscD features an extended conformation, while the domains of PrgH are in a more compact arrangement.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of crystal structures.

claim: The connecting hinge between the second and third periplasmic domains is mainly responsible for the high flexibility of YscD.
source: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that the connecting hinge (residues A282-N284) between the second and third periplasmic domains is mainly responsible for the high flexibility of YscD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: The G283P mutation resulted in a protein that was still functional for type III secretion in vivo.
source: Mutation of G283 to a proline resulted in a protein that was still functional for type III secretion in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by secretion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The 1.4 Å resolution crystal structure of YscD150–347 G283P had a slightly more bent conformation in the hinge region.
source: The 1.4 Å resolution crystal structure of YscD150–347 G283P had a slightly more bent conformation in the hinge region, but otherwise showed the same extended domain organization as YscD150–362wt: the first two domains superpose well with the wt structure, while the third domain is tilted by ∼9° with respect to the first two (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray crystallography data.

claim: The proline mutant has lower atomic B-factors and hence a more rigid, but still functional, structure.
source: Comparison of the dynamic mobility of each structure corroborated this; the proline mutant has lower atomic B-factors and hence a more rigid, but still functional, structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic B-factor analysis and functional assays.

claim: MD simulations showed that both straight and bent structures constitute stable conformational states for the YscD protein.
source: The simulations showed that both straight and bent structures constitute stable conformational states for the YscD protein.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: The application of stretching forces in MD produced an almost barrier-free transition from the compact to the extended conformation.
source: Moreover, the application of stretching forces in MD produced an almost barrier-free transition from the compact to the extended conformation, resulting in a domain arrangement similar to that observed by X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is supported by steered MD simulation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The periplasmic domains of YscD can undergo a maximal elongation of about 3.5 nm.
source: Due to this tertiary structure elasticity, that is, the rearrangement of tertiary structure in response to mechanical force, the periplasmic domains of YscD can undergo a maximal elongation of about 3.5 nm (i.e., a 50% elongation compared to the compact conformation), while opposing the stretching with a force as small as 35 ± 15 pN per YscD monomer, a value that is comparable with that estimated for other highly stretchable multi-domain proteins (Hsin and Schulten, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by steered MD simulation data.

claim: The tertiary structural elasticity of the ring components of the periplasmic portion of YscD significantly contributes to the overall elasticity of the basal body of the injectisome.
source: This suggests that the tertiary structural elasticity of the ring components of the periplasmic portion of YscD significantly contributes to the overall elasticity of the basal body of the injectisome in response to external forces.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation results showing YscD flexibility.

claim: A pseudo-atomic model of the inner membrane part of the basal body was constructed by combining experimental data with molecular modeling and simulations.
source: We constructed a pseudo-atomic model of the inner membrane part of the basal body by combining experimental data with molecular modeling and simulations, similar as to exercised previously to unveil the architecture of large macromolecular complexes (Alber et al., 2007; Lasker et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the integrative modeling approach used.

claim: Only an elongated arrangement of the C-terminal periplasmic domain of YscD best fits the in situ cryo-ET map.
source: The assembly of the YscDJ ring (Figure 4) revealed that only an elongated arrangement of the C-terminal periplasmic domain of YscD—similar to the X-ray structure—best fits the in situ cryo-ET map, extending up towards the position of the secretin ring.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling and fitting to the cryo-ET map.

claim: An average in situ structure of the Shigella flexneri injectisome was generated at ~7 nm resolution.
source: The structure of an isolated Ysc Yersinia injectisome is not available for comparison; therefore we examined Shigella flexneri bacteria by cryo-ET and generated an average in situ structure of the Shigella flexneri injectisome (Figure 5) at ∼7 nm resolution.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and FSC analysis.

claim: The S. flexneri injectisome has a length measurement between the centers of the membranes of 32 nm.
source: Nevertheless, despite the lower resolution, the map allows to reliably detect the positions of the membrane surrounding the injectisome, resulting in a length measurement between the centers of the membranes of 32 nm (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the cryo-ET reconstruction.

claim: Full-length YscC was expressed, purified, and reconstituted into liposomes.
source: To evaluate the contribution of the secretin YscC to the elasticity, we expressed and purified full-length YscC, reconstituted it into liposomes, and reconstructed its structure at a resolution of ∼3 nm by cryo-ET and sub-volume averaging (Figure 6).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for studying isolated YscC.

claim: The isolated and liposome-inserted YscC complexes showed several ring densities.
source: The isolated and liposome-inserted YscC complexes showed several ring densities: in the membrane bilayer, ∼5.5 nm below the membrane, and ∼12 nm below the membrane.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-ET reconstruction of isolated YscC.

claim: YscC undergoes a 30-40% length extension in the assembled injectisome with respect to its lipid vesicle-reconstituted state.
source: The described assignment of the YscC/YscD junction would correspond to a 30–40% length extension of YscC in the assembled injectisome, with respect to its lipid vesicle-reconstituted state (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of in situ and isolated structures.

claim: The Shigella injectisome in situ appeared about 10 nm or ~40% longer than isolated structures.
source: Yersinia injectisomes were found to vary in length by 20% inside the bacterial cells (an intermembrane distance between 30 and 36 nm). Most injectisomes seemed intact; nevertheless, we cannot exclude that under a certain osmotic pressure the injectisomes may detach from the outer membrane. Biophysical experiments would be required to understand, to which limits the basal body may stretch. In addition to the observed length variations, the injectisome's basal bodies were longer in the native context than suggested from single particle structures: the Shigella injectisome in situ appeared about 10 nm or ∼40% longer (32 nm vs 22 nm at the membrane level).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of in situ and isolated structures.

claim: Stretching of YscC by an estimated 5 nm and an elongation of YscD by an estimated 3.5 nm would explain an ~8.5 nm overall extension of the Yersinia injectisome's basal body.
source: Stretching of YscC by an estimated 5 nm and an elongation of YscD by an estimated 3.5 nm would explain an ∼8.5 nm overall extension of the Yersinia injectisome's basal body; the remaining 1.5 nm towards the observed 10 nm elongation of the Shigella system may be attributed to inter-species differences, or the limited resolution of the maps.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and simulation data.

claim: The isolated S. flexneri injectisome would have to be stretched by ~40% to match the dimensions of the average in situ Yersinia structure.
source: Even the shortest of our MRA class averages of in situ Yersinia injectisomes (Figure 2B) is still longer than the isolated Shigella injectisome, which would have to be stretched by ∼40% to match the dimensions of the average in situ Yersinia structure (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of structures shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The in situ reconstructions of the Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes show high overall similarity.
source: The in situ reconstructions of the Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes show high overall similarity considering the lower resolution of the Shigella injectisome: the overall dimensions, ring hierarchy and the peptidoglycan attachment location are conserved.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the two in situ structures.

claim: In the Yersinia injectisome, the torus ring assigned to YscV was ~5 nm below the membrane.
source: We could detect a significant difference in the location of the torus ring assigned to the N-terminus or YscV/MxiA (Abrusci et al., 2013). In the Yersinia injectisome, it was ∼5 nm below the membrane, while in the Shigella injectisome it was ∼10 nm below the membrane.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the reconstruction.

claim: In the Shigella injectisome, the torus ring assigned to MxiA was ~10 nm below the membrane.
source: We could detect a significant difference in the location of the torus ring assigned to the N-terminus or YscV/MxiA (Abrusci et al., 2013). In the Yersinia injectisome, it was ∼5 nm below the membrane, while in the Shigella injectisome it was ∼10 nm below the membrane.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the reconstruction.

claim: The in situ reconstructions of the Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes did not reveal obvious C-rings.
source: Injectisomes contain proteins homologous to FliN and FliM, termed YscQ in Yersinia and Spa33 in Shigella, which are suggested to form a C-ring (Morita-Ishihara et al., 2006) similar to bacterial flagellar motors. However, the in situ reconstructions of the Yersinia and Shigella injectisomes did not reveal obvious C-rings (Figure 2A,B and Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET reconstructions.

claim: YscQ could be unstructured or only transiently associated with the injectisome.
source: This could be caused by YscQ being unstructured, or being only transiently associated with the injectisome.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the absence of visible C-rings.

claim: Exposure of Y. enterocolitica bacteria to osmotic stress from high salt conditions resulted in a significant elongation of their basal bodies.
source: In order to influence the intermembrane distance, we placed Y. enterocolitica bacteria in high salt media (10-fold concentrated PBS; 10× PBS). The osmotic pressure experienced by the bacterial membranes (Koch, 1998) significantly widened the periplasmic space, while injectisomes remained in place and were studied by cryo-ET. The length of observed basal bodies increased by ∼10% (with statistical significance, Figure 7), while preserving the basal bodies seemingly intact.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Bacteria are likely exposed to considerable physical forces in vivo.
source: Bacteria are likely exposed to considerable physical forces in vivo, originating from swimming motions, contact with host cells, or from changes in osmolarity of the surrounding medium.
evidence: This is general knowledge about bacterial physiology.

claim: The observed elasticity might allow the injectisome to better cope with membrane stresses.
source: We hypothesize that the here observed elasticity might allow the injectisome to better cope with such membrane stresses.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed flexibility and osmotic stress experiments.

claim: The significantly larger basal bodies of flagellar motors do not vary in length.
source: Recently, it was suggested that injectisomes may rotate upon action (Ohgita et al., 2013), similarly to the evolutionary related flagellar motors. To our knowledge, however, the significantly larger basal bodies of flagellar motors do not vary in length, despite their active rotation.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of flagellar motor structures from the literature.

claim: The basal bodies of the bacterial flagellar motors do not seem to differ in dimensions between their isolated and in situ structures.
source: Furthermore, the basal bodies of the bacterial flagellar motors do not seem to differ in dimensions between their isolated and in situ structures (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on flagellar motors.

claim: For more fragile protein complexes that span two membranes, tertiary structure elasticity may constitute a general mechanism for structural protection.
source: We here hypothesize that for more fragile protein complexes that span two membranes, tertiary structure elasticity may constitute a general mechanism for structural protection.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings in this study.

claim: The channel of the injectisome's needle is resolved at the OM.
source: The channel of the injectisome's needle is resolved at the OM.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET reconstruction.

claim: A large ring-like structure can be discerned on the cytoplasmic side of the IM.
source: Further, a large ring-like structure can be discerned on the cytoplasmic side of the IM (Figure 2A, yellow).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET reconstruction shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A smaller, torus-like structure is localized ~5 nm underneath the membrane, which is tentatively proposed to be the export gate YscV.
source: It surrounds a smaller, torus-like structure localized ∼5 nm underneath the membrane, which we tentatively propose to be the export gate YscV (Figure 2A, red), based on the localization of the export gate protein FlhA of the flagella motor (Abrusci et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on analogy to the flagellar motor system.

claim: The density below the export gate likely corresponds to the YscN ATPase.
source: Similarly, in analogy to the flagellar motor system (Chen et al., 2011), the density below the export gate likely corresponds to the YscN ATPase.
evidence: This is an inference based on analogy to the flagellar motor system.

claim: The YscC-D junction is distinguishable in the density map.
source: The YscC-D junction is distinguishable in the density map and indicated in the density assignment (Figure 2A, asterisk).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-ET reconstruction.

claim: Most of the YscD/YscJ interactions occur between the first periplasmic domain of YscD and the C-terminal domain of YscJ.
source: Most of the YscD/YscJ interactions occur between the first periplasmic domain of YscD and the C-terminal domain of YscJ.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular modeling and assembly.

claim: The 24-meric YscD assembly is compatible with the basal body's diameter as observed by cryo-EM.
source: In particular, the 24-meric YscD assembly is compatible with the basal body's diameter, as observed by cryo-EM, while a higher number of YscD units would lead to a poorer match with the experimental data.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling and fitting to the cryo-ET map.

claim: The model constructed of 24 YscJ molecules does not produce gaps or overlaps in the final structural assembly.
source: Taking the observed stoichiometry of EscJ into account (Crepin et al., 2005; Yip et al., 2005), the model constructed of 24 YscJ molecules does not produce gaps or overlaps in the final structural assembly, as we otherwise obtained when using a higher or lower stoichiometry.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results and citations to EscJ stoichiometry.

claim: MD simulations suggested a limited fluctuation for the TM portion of YscD embedded in a membrane model.
source: MD simulations also suggested a limited fluctuation for this portion of YscD embedded in a membrane model, confirming the preferential orientation found in the 24-mer YscD ring assembly (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data.

claim: The cryo-ET density could be optimally fitted only by extended forms similar to the X-ray YscD conformation.
source: Although the cryo-ET density could be optimally fitted only by extended forms similar to the X-ray YscD conformation, MD snapshots of individual monomers in more compact forms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) allowed the construction, without incurring in steric clashes, of YscD 24-mer ring structures representative of possible states of intermediate compression compared to the fully extended ring model.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling and fitting to the cryo-ET map.
